questions.q: A glass workshop in Firozabad grinds and polishes a flat piece of glass into a curved bowl shape. A worker then applies a thin layer of aluminium on its outer, bulging curved surface. What has the workshop made, and from which surface will light reflect?
questions.a: A concave mirror; light reflects off the uncoated inner surface
o: A concave mirror; light reflects off the uncoated inner surface
A convex mirror; light reflects off the coated, outer bulging surface
A convex mirror; light reflects off the uncoated inner surface
A concave mirror; light reflects off the coated outer surface

questions.q:
At a science centre, Meena looked into a curved mirror and saw her own face unusually large. Her brother, standing a little farther away, looked upside down in the same mirror. Earlier, in Grade 7, she had seen that a plane mirror gives an image of the same size as the object and erect.
(a) Name the two features of the images in this curved mirror that a plane mirror never shows.
(b) Using (a), explain what the guide meant by saying that the image looks different because the mirror is curved inward or outward, and not flat.
questions.a: (a) Her face looked enlarged (larger than the object), and her brother's image was inverted (upside down). A plane mirror always gives an erect image of the same size. (b) Since a flat (plane) mirror can never give an enlarged or an inverted image, these images must come from the shape of the reflecting surface: it is curved (here, a spherical mirror), and a curved surface changes the size and orientation of the image.
s: (a) enlarged image and inverted image, neither of which a plane mirror forms
(b) so the reflecting surface must be curved, not flat; the curve changes size and orientation

questions.q:
Consider these statements about spherical mirrors and curved surfaces.
Statement 1: Spherical mirrors are made by slicing curved pieces off a hollow glass sphere.
Statement 2: A concave mirror and a convex mirror held close to a face both give an erect image that is smaller than the face.
Statement 3: The outer, bulging side of a shiny spoon gives an image of a face that is erect but smaller than the face.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 3 only
o: 3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
At a science centre in Bengaluru, three curved exhibit mirrors, X, Y and Z, have lost their name cards. A volunteer writes down what she sees.
Mirror X: viewed from the side at its level, the shiny face rises in the middle. A child standing close and a child standing far away both look erect and smaller.
Mirror Y: viewed from the side, the shiny face dips in the middle. A child standing close looks erect and larger; a child farther away looks upside down.
Mirror Z: viewed from the side, the shiny face rises in the middle. A child standing close looks erect and larger.
(a) Name mirrors X and Y, giving the shape evidence for each.
(b) Explain why the two observations recorded for Mirror Z cannot both be right.
(c) The centre can re-check only one mirror today. Decide which mirror it should be and name one observation that would settle what that mirror is.
questions.a: (a) X is a convex mirror: its reflecting surface curves outwards (rises in the middle). Y is a concave mirror: its reflecting surface curves inwards (dips in the middle). (b) A shiny face that rises in the middle curves outwards, which makes Z a convex mirror; but a convex mirror always gives an erect image smaller than the object, never a larger one. A larger, erect image of a close child happens with a concave mirror. So one of the two entries is wrong. (c) Re-check Z, because X and Y each have shape and image evidence that agree. Settle it by viewing Z from the side again at the level of its surface, or by looking at a child standing far away: if the far image is upside down the mirror is concave; if every image is erect and smaller it is convex.
s: (a) X convex (surface curves outward), Y concave (surface curves inward)
(b) rising surface means convex, but a convex mirror never gives an enlarged image; the entries conflict
(c) choose Z, since X and Y are consistent, and give one deciding check (side view again, or image of a far child: inverted means concave, always erect and smaller means convex)

questions.q: Kavya holds a steel ladle at arm's length and sees her face upside down in one of its sides. Which statement correctly names that side and predicts what she will see when she turns the ladle around?
questions.a: The inner side, curving inwards like a concave mirror; she will then see her face erect but smaller
o: The inner side, curving inwards like a concave mirror; she will then see her face erect but smaller
The outer side, curving outwards like a convex mirror; she will then see her face erect and larger
The inner side, curving inwards like a convex mirror; she will then see her face upside down again
The inner side, curving inwards like a concave mirror; she will then see her face erect and the same size

questions.q: True or false? 'If you turn a concave mirror over and look at its back, the coated surface you see curves inwards.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. A concave mirror is made by putting the reflective coating on the outer curved surface, so that light reflects off the inner surface, which curves inwards. The coated surface is therefore the outer one: seen from the back it bulges outwards, towards you.
s: verdict: false
reason: the coating of a concave mirror is on the outer curved surface, which bulges outward when seen from the back

questions.q: Arjun writes this rule in his notebook: 'Every curved mirror is a spherical mirror.' Is his rule correct? Give your verdict and explain what makes a mirror spherical. (You may use a shiny spoon as an example of a curved mirror.)
questions.a: No. The chapter calls spherical mirrors a common type of curved mirror, which means there are curved mirrors that are not spherical. A mirror is spherical only when its reflecting surface is spherical, that is, shaped like a part of a hollow sphere. A shiny spoon is curved and acts like a mirror, but the chapter only calls it a curved mirror; being curved is not enough to make a mirror spherical, so the rule claims too much.
s: verdict: no
spherical mirrors are one common type of curved mirror, not all of them
spherical means the reflecting surface is part of a hollow sphere; curved alone is not enough

questions.q:
Match each piece of evidence in Column I with what it tells you in Column II.
Column I
1. A ground glass piece coated on its inner curved surface
2. A toy held close to the mirror looks erect and larger
3. The image of a toy stays the same size at every distance
4. Seen from directly above, the mirror's outline is a circle
Column II
a. Plane mirror
b. Cannot tell the type from this alone
c. Convex mirror
d. Concave mirror

Rekha wrote this five-step guide for identifying an unlabelled mirror.
Step 1: Look from directly above. If the outline is a circle, the mirror is spherical; if not, it is plane.
Step 2: Look from the side, level with the shiny surface. If it dips in the middle, the mirror is concave; if it rises in the middle, it is convex.
Step 3: If a face held close looks larger than in real life, the mirror is concave.
Step 4: If a face held close looks erect, the mirror is convex.
Step 5: If an object far away looks upside down, the mirror is concave.
Judge each step as sound or faulty, and correct every faulty step.
questions.a: Step 1 faulty: spherical mirrors have a circular outline, but a plane mirror can be round too, so the outline cannot separate them; use the side view or the images instead. Step 2 sound: a surface dipping in the middle curves inwards (concave); one rising in the middle curves outwards (convex). Step 3 sound: only a concave mirror gives an enlarged image (close up); a plane mirror gives the same size and a convex mirror always a smaller one. Step 4 faulty: a face held close looks erect in all three mirrors (enlarged in concave, same size in plane, smaller in convex), so 'erect' alone does not show convex; check the size, and only 'erect and smaller' means convex. Step 5 sound: plane and convex mirrors always give erect images, so an inverted image can come only from a concave mirror.
s: Step 1 faulty: a plane mirror can also have a circular outline
Step 2 sound, with the reason (inward curve concave, outward convex)
Step 3 sound: only a concave mirror enlarges
Step 4 faulty: close images are erect in all three; size decides (erect and smaller = convex)
Step 5 sound: only a concave mirror can give an inverted image

questions.q: In a textbook diagram, light comes from the left. A mirror is drawn as an arc whose middle bulges towards the right, away from the light. Short slanting lines (shading) are drawn on the right-hand side of the arc. Which mirror does the diagram show?
questions.a: A concave mirror, because the unshaded side facing the light is hollow
o: A concave mirror, because the unshaded side facing the light is hollow
A convex mirror, because the arc bulges outwards towards the right-hand side
A convex mirror, because the shading shows the reflecting surface
A concave mirror, because the shading shows its reflecting surface

questions.q:
(a) A polished brass lota has a round, bulging body. Does the outside of its body behave like a concave or a convex mirror? Give the reason from the way the surface curves.
(b) Rani looks into the hollow inside of a polished steel katori. Which mirror does that surface behave like, and which surface of the same katori would behave like the type you named in (a)?
questions.a: (a) Convex: the shiny surface curves outwards (bulges towards the viewer), and a mirror whose reflecting surface curves outwards is convex. (b) The hollow inside curves inwards, so it behaves like a concave mirror. The outside of the katori (its bulging bottom and sides) curves outwards, so it behaves like a convex mirror, like the lota in (a).
s: (a) convex, because the reflecting surface curves outwards
(b) inside behaves as concave (curves inwards); the bulging outside behaves as convex

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Spherical mirrors for a school laboratory are made from flat pieces of glass rather than by cutting up a hollow glass sphere.
Reason (R): A spherical mirror is shaped like a part of an imaginary hollow sphere.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q: Show that the shiny inner side of a spoon, which curves inwards, cannot be behaving like a convex mirror. Use both the shape of the surface and the image of your face when the spoon is held at arm's length.
questions.a: Shape: a mirror whose reflecting surface curves inwards is, by definition, a concave mirror; a convex mirror's reflecting surface curves outwards. The inner side of the spoon curves inwards, so it fits only the concave description. Image: at arm's length the inner side shows the face inverted (upside down). A convex mirror always gives an erect image, so an inverted image rules out a convex mirror. Both pieces of evidence say the inner side behaves like a concave mirror, so it cannot be acting as a convex one.
s: inward-curving reflecting surface matches the concave definition, not convex (outward)
the inner side gives an inverted image at arm's length
a convex mirror always gives an erect image, so the inner side cannot be convex

questions.q: At a mela in Mysuru, a craftsman hangs a polished mirror shaped like a piece of a hollow sphere, with its bulging face turned towards the crowd. What will a child standing in the crowd see?
questions.a: Herself erect and smaller, since the bulging face acts as a convex mirror
o: Herself erect and smaller, since the bulging face acts as a convex mirror
Herself upside down, since every spherical mirror turns the images it forms over
Herself erect and the same size, since it is still a mirror
Herself erect and larger, since a curved face always magnifies

questions.q:
A 'funny mirrors' tent at a fair in Hyderabad has four mirrors. The caretaker's notes give the shape of each reflecting surface (seen from the side) and one visitor's comment.
P (in the middle of the tent; visitors can stand near it or far from it): surface dips in the middle. 'My nose looked huge when I went right up close.'
Q: surface rises in the middle. 'I looked small, even from close by.'
R: surface is flat. 'Just a normal reflection.'
S (on the far wall, behind a rope, so visitors can only see it from a distance): surface dips in the middle. 'From back here I am upside down.'
(a) Name the type of each mirror.
(b) P and S drew very different comments. Explain why, if they are the same type.
(c) The tent owner must remove one mirror to make space, but visitors must still be able to see every kind of image that the four mirrors gave. Decide which mirror to remove and justify.
questions.a: (a) P concave and S concave (surfaces curve inwards); Q convex (surface curves outwards); R plane. (b) A concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image of an object close to it, and an inverted image when the object is farther away; the visitor at P was right up close, while S can only be seen from a distance. (c) Remove S. P is also concave and visitors can stand far from it, so P alone can show both the enlarged, erect close-up and the inverted image from a distance; Q (always erect and smaller) and R (same size) are each the only mirror of their kind and must stay. Removing P would lose the close-up enlarged view, because visitors cannot get near S.
s: (a) P and S concave, Q convex, R plane
(b) same concave type: close up erect and enlarged, far away inverted
(c) remove S, because P can give both concave images while Q and R are unique and S cannot be approached

questions.q:
Ishita sees a tree far away upside down in a curved mirror. She writes: 'The reflecting surface of this mirror must curve outwards.'
(a) Which of the three kinds of mirror (plane, concave, convex) can give an inverted image?
(b) Use (a) to correct her conclusion.
questions.a: (a) Only a concave mirror; a plane mirror always gives an erect image, and a convex mirror always gives an erect image too. (b) Since the image is inverted, the mirror is concave, and a concave mirror's reflecting surface curves inwards, not outwards.
s: (a) only a concave mirror can give an inverted image; plane and convex images are always erect
(b) so the mirror is concave and its reflecting surface curves inwards

questions.q: The guide told Meena that the curved mirrors at the science centre were 'not plane mirrors'. Which of her observations would NOT, on its own, support the guide?
questions.a: In one mirror, her image looked erect
o: In one mirror, her image looked erect
In one mirror, her face looked unusually large
In one mirror, her brother looked upside down
In one mirror, she saw a tiny version of herself

questions.q:
Three students describe the same round mirror lying face up on a table.
Tara: 'Seen from above, its outline is a circle, so it is a plane mirror.'
Uday: 'Seen from the side, its shiny surface dips in the middle, so it is a concave mirror.'
Veer: 'My face held close looked erect in it, so it must be a convex mirror.'
Judge each student's reasoning.
questions.a: Tara is wrong: the outline of a spherical mirror is also circular, so a circular outline cannot show that a mirror is plane. Uday is right: a reflecting surface that dips in the middle curves inwards, which makes it a concave mirror. Veer's conclusion does not follow: a concave mirror also gives an erect image of a face held close (an enlarged one), and so does a plane mirror, so 'erect' alone cannot show that the mirror is convex; he should have checked whether the image was smaller or larger.
s: Tara wrong: spherical mirrors also have a circular outline
Uday right: surface dipping in the middle curves inward, so concave
Veer not justified: a concave mirror (and a plane mirror) also gives an erect image of a close face; the size decides

questions.q:
A worksheet shows a curved mirror drawn only as a plain arc, with no shading and no light rays.
(a) Why can a student not tell from this drawing whether the mirror is concave or convex?
(b) The teacher then adds shading on the hollow side of the arc. Which mirror is it now, and why?
questions.a: (a) The same arc has a hollow side and a bulging side, and either could be the reflecting surface; without knowing which side reflects, the drawing could stand for either mirror. (b) The shaded side shows the non-reflecting surface, so the reflecting surface is the bulging side, which curves outwards: it is a convex mirror.
s: (a) either side of the arc could be the reflecting surface, so the type is not fixed
(b) shading marks the non-reflecting hollow side, so the bulging side reflects: convex

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Nagpur made a poster on curved mirrors. It has five lines.
Line 1: A curved mirror always gives an image of a different size from the object.
Line 2: The inner side of a spoon behaves like a concave mirror, and its outer side like a convex mirror.
Line 3: Because a spherical mirror is part of a hollow sphere, its outline seen from the front is circular.
Line 4: A convex mirror bulges towards the object, so the image it gives is larger than the object.
Line 5: In a diagram of a concave mirror, the shading is drawn on the side facing the incoming light.
Judge each line as correct or wrong, and rewrite every wrong line correctly.
questions.a: Line 1 wrong: an image formed by a concave mirror can be enlarged, diminished or of the same size as the object, depending on the object's distance, so 'always different' is wrong. Line 2 correct: the inner side curves inwards (concave) and the outer side bulges outwards (convex). Line 3 correct: the chapter says the outline of a spherical mirror's surface is circular. Line 4 wrong: a convex mirror does bulge outwards, but its image is always smaller than the object (and erect). Line 5 wrong: the shading shows the non-reflecting surface, which is the back, facing away from the incoming light; the reflecting hollow side faces the light.
s: Line 1 wrong: a concave mirror can also give a same-size image
Line 2 correct, with the reason
Line 3 correct, with the reason
Line 4 wrong: a convex mirror's image is always smaller
Line 5 wrong: shading marks the non-reflecting back, away from the light

questions.q: Some jobs need an enlarged, erect view of a small thing held close. Describe one such everyday job (other than a dentist's). Name the mirror you would give that person, say how close the thing must be held, and explain why the other two kinds of mirror would not do.
questions.a: Any suitable job, such as a jeweller checking the tiny clasp of a chain, or a watch repairer looking at a small part. Give a concave mirror and hold the object close to it, because a concave mirror forms an erect, enlarged image when the object is close (farther away the image turns inverted). A plane mirror only gives an image of the same size, and a convex mirror always gives a smaller image, so neither enlarges the small part.
s: a valid new job needing an enlarged, erect view of a small close object
concave mirror, held close, because it then gives an erect, enlarged image
plane gives same size and convex always smaller, so neither enlarges

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The reflector behind the bulb of a torch is a concave mirror.
Reason (R): A concave mirror always forms an image smaller than the object.
questions.a: A is true, but R is false
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Kanpur did the image activity with a plane, a concave and a convex mirror standing side by side, a small toy and a ruler. Their record:
Plane mirror: toy at 4 cm - erect, same size; toy at 80 cm - erect, same size; lateral inversion - yes.
Concave mirror: toy at 4 cm - erect, enlarged; toy at 80 cm - erect, smaller; lateral inversion - yes.
Convex mirror: toy at 4 cm - erect, smaller; toy at 80 cm - erect, slightly smaller still; lateral inversion - no.
(a) One entry in the concave row is wrong. Find it and correct it.
(b) One entry in the lateral-inversion column is wrong. Find it and correct it.
(c) Rohan says the plane-mirror entry at 80 cm must be wrong, because a farther toy should look smaller in the mirror. Judge his objection.
(d) The group has time to repeat only one distance. Using the corrected record, decide which distance gives three different image sizes in the three mirrors, and justify.
questions.a: (a) The concave mirror at 80 cm: when the toy is moved farther away the image becomes inverted, so it should read 'inverted' (here smaller), not erect. (b) The convex row: lateral inversion is seen in all three types of mirror, so it should be 'yes'. (c) Rohan is wrong: a plane mirror always forms an erect image of the same size as the object, whatever the distance; only spherical mirrors change the image size with distance. (d) 4 cm: the plane mirror gives the same size, the concave mirror an enlarged image and the convex mirror a smaller image, three different sizes. At 80 cm both the concave and the convex images are smaller, so the sizes do not all differ.
s: (a) concave at 80 cm should be inverted, not erect
(b) convex lateral inversion should be yes; it occurs in all three mirrors
(c) objection wrong: a plane mirror always gives a same-size erect image
(d) 4 cm, since sizes are same, enlarged and smaller; at 80 cm two are smaller

questions.q: A supplier has only concave mirrors in stock. For which of these orders would a concave mirror NOT be the right kind?
questions.a: A mirror to watch all the aisles of a big store at once
o: A mirror to watch all the aisles of a big store at once
A reflector to fit behind the bulb of a scooter headlight
The large main mirror of a reflecting telescope
A reflector to fit behind the bulb of a torch

questions.q:
A toy is moved away from a plane mirror, a concave mirror and a convex mirror until the concave mirror's image has just turned inverted. The images in the other two mirrors are still erect.
(a) What one observation tells the plane-mirror image and the convex-mirror image apart at this distance?
(b) Ravi says, 'Now that the concave mirror's image has turned inverted, it must also be smaller than the toy.' Judge his statement.
questions.a: (a) The size: the plane mirror's image is the same size as the toy, while the convex mirror's image is smaller than the toy. (b) Ravi is wrong: when the image of a concave mirror first becomes inverted it is still enlarged; it becomes smaller only as the toy is moved still farther away.
s: (a) size: plane same size, convex smaller
(b) wrong: just after turning inverted the concave image is still enlarged, shrinking only farther away

questions.q: At a fun fair, Sana stands 1 m from a curved mirror and then 4 m from it. Both times she looks erect and smaller than herself; at 4 m she looks only slightly smaller than at 1 m. Which mirror is this?
questions.a: A convex mirror
o: A convex mirror
A concave mirror, as the size changes with distance
A plane mirror, as the image stays erect
A concave mirror, as the image keeps shrinking

questions.q:
At one curved mirror in the science centre, Meena saw 'a tiny version of herself'. The guide said that, from size alone, it could be either a concave or a convex mirror.
(a) Which one feature of the tiny image would settle the question?
(b) State what each possible answer would show.
questions.a: (a) Whether the tiny image is erect or inverted (upside down). (b) If it is erect, the mirror is convex (a convex mirror always gives an erect, diminished image). If it is inverted, the mirror is concave and she was standing far from it (a concave mirror gives an inverted image, which keeps getting smaller as the object moves away).
s: (a) the orientation: erect or inverted
(b) erect means convex; inverted means concave with her standing far away

questions.q: A toy is kept 3 cm in front of each of three mirrors standing side by side: a plane mirror, a concave mirror and a convex mirror. The number of these mirrors that show an image larger than the toy is ___. (Write a number.)

(a) A tailor's shop wants a mirror in which customers see themselves erect and at their true size while trying on clothes. Which kind of mirror should it use?
(b) Customers stand at different distances from the mirror. Using (a), explain why a concave mirror would not do this job.
questions.a: (a) A plane mirror, because it always forms an erect image of the same size as the object, at every distance. (b) In a concave mirror the image changes with distance: a customer standing close would look erect but enlarged, and one standing farther away would look inverted; so customers would not see themselves at true size and erect.
s: (a) plane mirror: erect and same size at every distance
(b) concave image changes with distance: enlarged close up, inverted farther away

questions.q: Pari stands close to each of three mirrors in turn, a plane mirror, a concave mirror and a convex mirror, and raises her right hand. For each mirror, say whether her image is erect or inverted, whether it is larger, smaller or the same size, and which hand her image appears to raise.
questions.a: Plane mirror: erect, the same size, and the image appears to raise its left hand. Concave mirror (she is close to it): erect and enlarged, and the image appears to raise its left hand. Convex mirror: erect and smaller, and the image appears to raise its left hand. Lateral inversion (left and right swapped) is seen in all three types of mirror, so the raised hand looks like the left hand in each.
s: plane: erect, same size
concave (close): erect, enlarged; convex: erect, smaller
in all three the image appears to raise the left hand, since lateral inversion occurs in every mirror

questions.q:
A student recorded the image of a candle in one concave mirror at five distances (illustrative values; 'times' compares the image's height with the candle's).
5 cm: erect, 2 times
15 cm: inverted, 2 times
20 cm: inverted, 1 time
30 cm: inverted, 0.5 times
40 cm: inverted, about one-third
(a) The chapter's summary says a concave mirror's image can be enlarged, diminished or of the same size as the object. Point to the readings that show each.
(b) At 20 cm the image is the same size as the candle. Is it the same as the image a plane mirror gives? Explain.
(c) Predict the image at 35 cm, and justify from the table.
(d) Sohail sees a same-size image of a candle in an unknown mirror and says, 'It must be a plane mirror.' Use this table to explain why that is not certain.
(e) What single extra observation of that same-size image would settle Sohail's question?
questions.a: (a) Enlarged: 5 cm and 15 cm (2 times); same size: 20 cm (1 time); diminished: 30 cm and 40 cm (0.5 times and about one-third). (b) No: the plane mirror's image is erect, while this same-size image is inverted. (c) Inverted and smaller than the candle, between one-half and one-third of its height: once inverted, the image keeps getting smaller as the candle moves away, and 35 cm lies between 30 cm and 40 cm. (d) A concave mirror can also give a same-size image (at 20 cm here), so 'same size' alone does not prove a plane mirror. (e) Whether the image is erect or inverted: an inverted same-size image means a concave mirror, while a plane mirror's same-size image is always erect.
s: (a) enlarged at 5 and 15 cm, same size at 20 cm, diminished at 30 and 40 cm
(b) not the same: this one is inverted, a plane mirror's is erect
(c) inverted, between 0.5 and about one-third of the height
(d) a concave mirror can also give a same-size image
(e) check orientation: inverted means concave, erect fits a plane mirror

questions.q:
(a) A dentist holds a small concave mirror close to a tooth inside a patient's mouth. Describe the image she sees and say why this helps her.
(b) Using (a), predict what would happen to the image if she held the same mirror far from the tooth, and why that would not help her.
questions.a: (a) An erect and enlarged image of the tooth, so she can inspect it in detail. (b) As the distance from a concave mirror increases, the image becomes inverted and then keeps getting smaller, so she would lose the erect, enlarged view she needs; that is why the mirror is held close.
s: (a) erect, enlarged image of the tooth, giving a detailed view
(b) far away the image turns inverted and then smaller, losing the enlarged erect view

questions.q: True or false? 'Like a concave mirror, a convex mirror will show an object upside down once the object is far enough away.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. A convex mirror always forms an erect image that is smaller than the object; as the object moves away the image only gets slightly smaller. Only a concave mirror turns the image upside down when the object is moved farther away.
s: verdict: false
reason: a convex mirror's image is always erect (and diminished); only a concave mirror inverts far objects

questions.q:
A student kept a pencil at different distances from two mirrors, M and N, and recorded the image (distances are illustrative).
Mirror M: 3 cm - erect, larger; 10 cm - erect, larger; 25 cm - inverted, larger; 50 cm - inverted, smaller; 100 cm - inverted, smaller still.
Mirror N: 3 cm - erect, smaller; 10 cm - erect, smaller; 25 cm - erect, smaller; 50 cm - erect, slightly smaller; 100 cm - erect, slightly smaller still.
(a) Identify mirror M, quoting two pieces of evidence from its row.
(b) Identify mirror N, quoting its evidence.
(c) Which mirror, used over which range of the recorded distances, could serve as a dentist's mirror? Explain.
(d) The reading for M at 150 cm was left blank. Predict it and justify.
(e) Pooja says, 'Mirror N is useless because it never makes anything bigger.' Give one use from the chapter where N's behaviour is exactly what is needed, and why.
questions.a: (a) M is a concave mirror: close up (3 cm, 10 cm) the image is erect and enlarged, and farther away it becomes inverted, first enlarged (25 cm) and then smaller. (b) N is a convex mirror: the image is erect and smaller at every distance and gets only slightly smaller as the pencil moves away. (c) Mirror M at the close distances, 3 cm to 10 cm, because there it gives an erect, enlarged image, which is what a dentist needs when the mirror is held close to the teeth. (d) Inverted and smaller than at 100 cm, because once the image of a concave mirror is inverted it keeps getting smaller as the object moves farther away. (e) A side-view mirror on a vehicle (or a road-safety or store mirror): it always gives an erect image of the traffic behind, and because it curves outwards it shows a much wider area of the road; being smaller is the price of seeing more.
s: (a) M concave: erect and enlarged close, inverted farther
(b) N convex: always erect and smaller, slightly smaller with distance
(c) M at 3-10 cm, where the image is erect and enlarged
(d) inverted and smaller than at 100 cm, since the inverted image keeps shrinking
(e) a valid convex use (side-view, road-safety or store mirror) with the reason: erect image, wider area

questions.q: Neha says, 'Without touching a mirror or looking at it from the side, I can tell whether it is plane, concave or convex just by watching the image of one object as I move the object closer and farther.' Is Neha right? Give your verdict and describe what she would see in each mirror.
questions.a: Yes. The chapter itself says the type of mirror can be identified from the images it forms. Plane mirror: the image stays erect and the same size at every distance. Convex mirror: the image is always erect and smaller than the object, getting only slightly smaller as the object moves away. Concave mirror: the image is erect and enlarged when the object is close and becomes inverted when the object is moved farther away. These three patterns are all different, so the images alone are enough.
s: verdict: yes
plane: erect and same size always; convex: always erect and smaller
concave: erect and enlarged close, inverted farther away, so all three patterns differ

questions.q: A visitor at a science centre sees an image of herself that is exactly her own size but upside down. Which mirror can give such an image?
questions.a: A concave mirror, with her at a suitable distance
o: A concave mirror, with her at a suitable distance
A plane mirror, whatever her distance from it
A convex mirror, with her standing far away
None, since a same-size image is always erect

questions.q:
A photographer in Guwahati took four photos of the same toy in one curved mirror, moving the toy farther from the mirror between shots, but the photos got shuffled.
Photo A: inverted, a little smaller than the toy
Photo B: erect, enlarged
Photo C: inverted, much smaller than the toy
Photo D: inverted, enlarged
(a) Which kind of mirror was used? Give the evidence from the photos.
(b) Arrange the photos in order, from the toy nearest the mirror to the toy farthest away, and explain the order.
(c) A fifth photo in the same folder shows the toy erect and smaller. Show that it cannot have come from this mirror.
(d) One more photo was taken with the toy even farther away than in Photo C, but it was lost. Predict what it showed and justify.
questions.a: (a) A concave mirror: the same mirror gave both erect and inverted images, and enlarged as well as smaller ones; plane and convex mirrors always give erect images. (b) B, D, A, C. Close to a concave mirror the image is erect and enlarged (B); farther away it becomes inverted, enlarged at first (D) and then keeps getting smaller (A, then C). (c) In a concave mirror, the image is erect only when the object is close, and then it is enlarged; once it gets smaller it is inverted. An erect, smaller image is what a convex mirror gives, so the fifth photo came from a different mirror. (d) Inverted and even smaller than in Photo C, because the inverted image keeps getting smaller as the toy moves farther away.
s: (a) concave: both erect and inverted images from one mirror
(b) order B, D, A, C with the reason
(c) a concave mirror's erect image is always enlarged, so erect and smaller cannot come from it
(d) inverted and smaller than in Photo C

questions.q: For a sharp bend on a hill road near Nainital, the council can fix either a plane mirror or a convex mirror of the same size. A councillor prefers the plane mirror because 'cars look their true size in it'. Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Choose the convex mirror: it shows a much wider stretch of road, though cars look smaller
o: Choose the convex mirror: it shows a much wider stretch of road, though cars look smaller
Choose the plane mirror: true size matters far more than how much of the bend's road is seen
Choose the convex mirror: it makes the oncoming cars look larger and easier to spot
Choose the plane mirror: a convex mirror would show oncoming cars upside down
