Consider these statements about images in mirrors.
Statement 1: Lateral inversion is seen in a plane mirror but not in spherical mirrors.
Statement 2: The image of a car in a convex mirror becomes slightly smaller as the car moves away.
Statement 3: When an object is far from a concave mirror, its image is inverted.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Four students describe images they claim to have seen in the convex side-view mirror of a parked scooter. Which description can NOT be right?
questions.a: A car far behind looked inverted and smaller
o: A car far behind looked inverted and smaller
A car far behind looked erect and smaller
A car moving away looked slightly smaller each moment
The word on a bus behind looked laterally inverted

questions.q:
The librarian of a school in Mysuru wants one mirror high in a corner of the library. Her main need is to notice at a glance whether anyone is in any of the six aisles. She tries two mirrors of the same size from her desk (notes are illustrative).
Mirror 1: all six aisles visible; every reader looks erect and small.
Mirror 2: only two aisles visible; a reader standing near the mirror (about 2 m away) looks erect and large, so she can see what he is reading; readers farther away look upside down.
(a) Which mirror is concave? Use both observations of Mirror 2.
(b) Which mirror is convex, and why does it show so many more aisles?
(c) Decide which mirror she should fix, weighing what each one offers against her main need, and state what she gives up.
questions.a: (a) Mirror 2: a concave mirror gives an erect, enlarged image of a close object and an inverted image of a farther one, which matches the reader near it and the readers far away. (b) Mirror 1: its images are always erect and smaller, and because a convex mirror curves outwards it shows a much wider area (as stores use it to monitor a large area). (c) Mirror 1, the convex mirror. Her main need is to see every aisle, and only Mirror 1 shows all six, with erect images. Mirror 2's large, clear view of a nearby reader is a real advantage, but it covers only two aisles and turns farther readers upside down. She gives up that large, detailed view of readers; in Mirror 1 everyone looks small.
s: (a) Mirror 2 concave: erect enlarged near, inverted far
(b) Mirror 1 convex: curving outward gives a much wider view
(c) choose Mirror 1 because it covers all aisles, giving up the large close-up view Mirror 2 offers

questions.q:
Consider these statements about reflection.
Statement 1: At the point where a ray strikes a convex mirror, the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
Statement 2: The angle of incidence is the angle between the incident ray and the surface of the mirror.
Statement 3: Astronomers in the time of Bhaskara II wrote down the two laws of reflection in their books.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A thin beam falls on a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 38 degrees. The torch is then moved so that the reflected beam turns 12 degrees closer to the normal. The new angle of incidence is ___ degrees. (Write a number.)

Two thin beams from different directions strike the same point O of a plane mirror. Both incident beams are on the left side of the normal at O; one has an angle of incidence of 30 degrees and the other 50 degrees.
(a) Why is the normal the same for both beams?
(b) Find the angle between the two reflected beams.
questions.a: (a) The normal is the line at 90 degrees to the mirror at the point of incidence; both beams fall at the same point O, so they share the same normal. (b) Both reflected beams go to the right of the normal, at 30 degrees and 50 degrees from it (r = i), so the angle between them is 50 - 30 = 20 degrees.
s: (a) same point of incidence, so the same perpendicular line is the normal
(b) reflected beams at 30 and 50 degrees on the same side; 50 - 30 = 20 degrees

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with what it shows in Column II.
Column I
1. Two beams strike the same point of a plane mirror from the same side of the normal, with angles of incidence 20 degrees and 50 degrees
2. The reflected beam disappears from the bent part of the chart paper
3. A ray strikes a convex mirror 30 degrees from the normal at that point
4. Table 10.1 shows 40 degrees for the angle of incidence and 41 degrees for the angle of reflection
Column II
a. The two reflected beams are 30 degrees apart
b. The incident ray, normal and reflected ray lie in one plane
c. The reflected ray leaves 30 degrees from that normal
d. The angles are equal; the gap is a measuring error

Assertion (A): A thin beam of light that falls on a plane mirror along the normal goes back along the same path.
Reason (R): For such a beam, the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are both zero.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A teacher in Raipur offers two set-ups for one lesson.
Set-up 1: A plane mirror stands upright on a white sheet. A thin beam from a torch with a comb slit falls on it; the incident and reflected beams and the normal are drawn, and both angles are measured with a protractor for five different angles.
Set-up 2: The same mirror and beam, but on a stiff chart paper that extends beyond the edge of the table; the reflected beam is watched on the extended part as that part is bent down along the table edge and then flattened again.
Today the protractors are locked away.
(a) Decide which set-up can still be carried out fully today, which law of reflection it tests, and why the other set-up cannot be finished.
(b) In Set-up 2, Manish sees the reflected beam vanish from the bent part and says the mirror has stopped reflecting. Correct him.
(c) Mehak asks what would happen if the extended part were bent upwards instead of downwards. Predict the result and explain what it shows about the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray.
questions.a: (a) Set-up 2: it needs no measurement of angles, only watching whether the reflected beam stays on the paper, and it tests the second law (the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in the same plane). Set-up 1 tests the first law by comparing the angles of incidence and reflection, which cannot be measured without a protractor. (b) The mirror is still reflecting: the beam reappears when the paper is flattened. The reflected beam stays in the plane of the incident beam; bending the paper makes a new plane, so the beam no longer falls on the bent part. (c) The beam would again not be seen on the bent part, because bending in either direction moves that part out of the plane of the incident beam. This shows that the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in one plane, whichever way the paper is bent.
s: (a) Set-up 2, which needs no angle measurement and tests the second law; Set-up 1 needs a protractor to compare angles
(b) the mirror still reflects; the bent part is a new plane, and the beam reappears when flattened
(c) beam again not seen, as any bend leaves the plane; so the three rays lie in one plane

questions.q: Arun keeps a plane mirror fixed and moves his torch so that the angle of incidence changes from 30 degrees to 50 degrees. What happens to the reflected beam?
questions.a: It turns 20 degrees farther away from the normal
o: It turns 20 degrees farther away from the normal
It turns 20 degrees closer towards the normal
It stays where it was, since the mirror has not moved
It turns 40 degrees farther away from the normal

questions.q: Sahil says, 'If I double the angle of incidence on a plane mirror, then the angle of reflection doubles, and the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror surface doubles too.' Test his claim using an angle of incidence of 20 degrees changed to 40 degrees, and give your verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. The angle of reflection always equals the angle of incidence, so it goes from 20 to 40 degrees: it doubles. But the reflected ray makes an angle of 90 minus r with the mirror surface (the normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror): 90 - 20 = 70 degrees at first and 90 - 40 = 50 degrees afterwards. It falls instead of doubling. So the first half of the claim is right and the second half is wrong.
s: r = i, so r goes from 20 to 40 degrees: first half right
angle with mirror = 90 - r: 70 degrees then 50 degrees, so it does not double
verdict: partly right

questions.q: A thin beam of light strikes a shiny convex mirror at a point P. Which statement about what happens at P is NOT correct?
questions.a: The laws of reflection do not apply, because the mirror is curved
o: The laws of reflection do not apply, because the mirror is curved
The normal at P is drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror surface at P
The angle of incidence at P equals the angle of reflection at P
The incident ray, the normal at P and the reflected ray lie in one plane

questions.q:
Asha drew the normal carelessly in the plane-mirror activity and measured an angle of incidence of 52 degrees and an angle of reflection of 28 degrees. The mirror obeys the laws of reflection.
(a) Find the true angle of incidence.
(b) By how many degrees was her normal tilted from the true normal?
questions.a: (a) Tilting the normal adds to one angle exactly what it takes from the other, so the sum of the two angles is unchanged: 52 + 28 = 80 degrees. Since the true angles are equal, each is 80 / 2 = 40 degrees. (b) 52 - 40 = 12 degrees (equally, 40 - 28 = 12 degrees).
s: (a) true angles equal and the sum is unchanged: (52 + 28) / 2 = 40 degrees
(b) tilt = 52 - 40 = 12 degrees

questions.q: More than 800 years ago, around the time of the mathematician Bhaskara II, astronomers looked at the reflected images of stars and planets in shallow bowls of water, through tubes placed at suitable angles, and measured the positions of these objects in the sky. The image can be seen through a tube only when the tube lies along the light reflected from the water. The laws of reflection were not written down then. Explain how this method depends on reflection, and why it suggests that the astronomers understood reflection in practice.
questions.a: The still water surface in the bowl acts as a mirror, so starlight falling on it is reflected and an image of the star is seen in the water. The image can be seen through the tube only if the tube lies along the reflected ray, so the tube has to be set at the angle at which the light leaves the water, which depends on the angle at which the starlight falls on it. Since they could place the tubes at the right angles and use them to measure positions reliably, their method behaved as if they knew how the reflected light's direction is linked to the incoming light's direction (the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection), even though they never stated the laws.
s: the water surface acts as a mirror reflecting the starlight
the tube must lie along the reflected ray, whose direction depends on the incoming light's direction
setting tubes at the right angles to measure positions shows a working grasp of the laws, though unwritten

questions.q:
An astronomy club in Ujjain recreates the old bowl-of-water method. The water surface is flat and level, so the normal to it is a vertical line. A bright star is 40 degrees above the horizon. Its light falls on the water, and a viewing tube must be pointed down at the water along the reflected light.
(a) Find the angle of incidence of the starlight on the water.
(b) Find the angle of reflection.
(c) At what angle below the horizontal must the tube point?
(d) Two hours later the star is 60 degrees above the horizon. Find the new angle of incidence and the new tilt of the tube below the horizontal.
(e) Which law of reflection tells the club that the tube must face the same direction (towards the same part of the sky) as the star, and not off to one side? Explain.
questions.a: (a) The starlight comes down at 40 degrees to the level water, so it makes 90 - 40 = 50 degrees with the vertical normal: angle of incidence = 50 degrees. (b) Angle of reflection = angle of incidence = 50 degrees. (c) The reflected light leaves at 50 degrees from the vertical, that is 90 - 50 = 40 degrees from the level surface, so the tube must point 40 degrees below the horizontal. (d) New angle of incidence = 90 - 60 = 30 degrees; the reflected ray is 30 degrees from the vertical, so the tube tilts 90 - 30 = 60 degrees below the horizontal. (e) The second law: the incident ray, the normal at the point of incidence and the reflected ray all lie in the same plane. The vertical normal and the incoming starlight fix one upright plane, so the reflected ray, and the tube, must lie in that same plane, facing the star's side of the sky.
s: (a) i = 90 - 40 = 50 degrees
(b) r = i = 50 degrees
(c) tube 90 - 50 = 40 degrees below the horizontal
(d) i = 30 degrees; tube 60 degrees below the horizontal
(e) second law: incident ray, normal and reflected ray in one plane, so the tube lies in the star's plane

questions.q: In a dark room, a thin beam of light falls on a plane mirror at an angle of incidence of 35 degrees. What is the angle between the incident beam and the reflected beam?
questions.a: 70 degrees
o: 70 degrees
35 degrees
55 degrees
110 degrees

questions.q:
A thin beam strikes a concave mirror at a point P. The normal at P is drawn at 90 degrees to the mirror's surface there, and the beam makes 25 degrees with this normal.
(a) What is the angle of reflection at P?
(b) Gita says, 'The laws of reflection were found with a plane mirror, so they cannot be used for a curved mirror.' Correct her.
questions.a: (a) 25 degrees, because the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. (b) The laws of reflection are valid for all kinds of mirrors, plane, concave and convex; at each point of a curved mirror, the ray obeys them using the normal at that point.
s: (a) r = i = 25 degrees
(b) the laws hold for all mirrors, applied with the normal at the point of incidence

questions.q:
At a science fair in Patna, a thin beam from a torch fitted with a comb slit falls on a plane mirror standing upright on a sheet of paper, and the reflected beam lands on a target. A visitor later finds only the two pencil lines on the paper and the protractor note: 'angle between the incident beam and the reflected beam = 112 degrees'. The mirror's position is marked.
(a) Find the angle of reflection.
(b) Working backwards, find the angle the incident beam made with the surface of the mirror.
(c) If the torch had been turned so that the angle of incidence became 40 degrees, find the new angle between the incident and reflected beams.
(d) The organiser now wants the reflected beam to go straight back into the torch. Decide where the torch must point and what the angles of incidence and reflection will then be.
questions.a: (a) Since i = r, the normal divides the 112 degrees equally: r = 112 / 2 = 56 degrees. (b) The angle of incidence is also 56 degrees, measured from the normal; the normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror, so the incident beam made 90 - 56 = 34 degrees with the mirror surface. (c) 40 + 40 = 80 degrees. (d) The torch must point along the normal, at 90 degrees to the mirror surface; then the angle of incidence and the angle of reflection are both 0 degrees and the beam returns along its own path.
s: (a) r = 112 / 2 = 56 degrees, as i = r
(b) i = 56 degrees from the normal, so 90 - 56 = 34 degrees with the mirror
(c) 2 x 40 = 80 degrees
(d) aim along the normal; i = r = 0 and the beam comes straight back

questions.q: Nisha's Table 10.1 from the plane-mirror activity reads: angle of incidence 20 degrees, angle of reflection 21 degrees; 40 degrees, 39 degrees; 60 degrees, 60 degrees. What should she conclude?
questions.a: The two angles are equal; the small gaps are errors in measuring
o: The two angles are equal; the small gaps are errors in measuring
The angle of reflection is always slightly larger than the angle of incidence
The angles are equal only at large angles such as 60 degrees
The angle of reflection depends on the mirror, not on the incident ray

questions.q: A student's notebook says: 'Angle of incidence = 35 degrees, angle of reflection = 35 degrees, angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray = 90 degrees.' Show that these three entries cannot all be correct, and suggest which kind of slip could explain it.
questions.a: The incident ray and the reflected ray lie on either side of the normal, so the angle between them is i + r. With i = r = 35 degrees, the angle between them must be 35 + 35 = 70 degrees, not 90 degrees. So at least one entry is wrong. A likely slip: the student measured one of the angles wrongly (for example the 90 degrees is really the angle the normal makes with the mirror), or measured the angle between the rays carelessly; so either the third entry should be 70 degrees, or, if the 90 degrees between the rays was measured correctly, the angles of incidence and reflection were misread and should each be 45 degrees.
s: angle between the rays = i + r, on either side of the normal
35 + 35 = 70 degrees, not 90 degrees, so the entries conflict
a reasonable correction: either the third entry should be 70 degrees, or (if 90 degrees between the rays is right) each angle should be 45 degrees

questions.q:
(a) A thin beam has an angle of incidence of 25 degrees on a plane mirror. Find the angles that the incident ray and the reflected ray each make with the mirror surface.
(b) Kavi measured the incident ray from the normal (25 degrees) but the reflected ray from the mirror surface (65 degrees), and wrote, 'The angles are not equal, so the law fails here.' Using (a), judge his conclusion.
questions.a: (a) The normal is at 90 degrees to the mirror, so each ray makes 90 - 25 = 65 degrees with the surface (the reflected ray also has r = 25 degrees). (b) His conclusion is wrong: he measured the two angles from different lines. A reflected ray at 65 degrees from the surface is 90 - 65 = 25 degrees from the normal, equal to the angle of incidence, so his readings agree with the law.
s: (a) both rays make 90 - 25 = 65 degrees with the surface
(b) wrong: 65 degrees from the surface is 25 degrees from the normal, so i = r holds

questions.q:
A group recorded these readings for a thin beam on a plane mirror (illustrative).
Trial 1: angle of incidence 20 degrees, angle of reflection 70 degrees
Trial 2: 30 degrees, 31 degrees
Trial 3: 45 degrees, 45 degrees
Trial 4: 0 degrees, 0 degrees
Trial 5: 55 degrees, 54 degrees
(a) Which trial is clearly out of line with the rest?
(b) Suggest the measuring slip that explains it, and correct the reading.
(c) Should Trials 2 and 5 be thrown out as well? Justify.
(d) What was the beam doing in Trial 4, and how would the reflected beam have looked?
(e) State the law the corrected table supports, and name the other law of reflection that this table cannot test, with the reason.
questions.a: (a) Trial 1. (b) 70 degrees is what you get if the angle is measured from the mirror surface instead of from the normal: 90 - 70 = 20 degrees, so the angle of reflection is really 20 degrees, equal to the angle of incidence. (c) No: 30 and 31, 55 and 54 are nearly equal, and the chapter says the angles come out nearly equal in practice and equal when measured carefully; a one-degree gap is a small measuring error. (d) The beam was falling along the normal; it was reflected straight back along its own path. (e) The angle of incidence is equal to the angle of reflection. It cannot test the second law, that the incident ray, the normal and the reflected ray lie in the same plane, because every reading was taken on one flat sheet; testing it needs the sheet to be bent, as when the reflected beam disappears from the bent part.
s: (a) Trial 1 is out of line
(b) angle measured from the mirror, not the normal; corrected r = 90 - 70 = 20 degrees
(c) keep Trials 2 and 5: nearly equal values within measuring error
(d) beam along the normal, reflected straight back
(e) first law supported; second law (same plane) untested because the sheet was never bent

questions.q:
A ray of light falls on a plane mirror and the reflected ray is seen to leave the mirror at 90 degrees to its surface.
(a) What are the angle of reflection and the angle of incidence?
(b) Ritu says, 'When light falls along the normal there is no angle at all, so no reflection takes place.' Using (a), correct her.
questions.a: (a) A ray at 90 degrees to the mirror lies along the normal, so the angle of reflection is 0 degrees; since the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, the angle of incidence is also 0 degrees. (b) Reflection does take place: the angles are zero, not missing. The light is reflected straight back along the normal, the same line it came in on, which still obeys the law i = r (0 = 0).
s: (a) reflected ray along the normal, so r = 0 and i = 0
(b) reflection still happens: the light returns along the normal, with i = r = 0

questions.q: True or false? 'Every ray of a parallel beam obeys the laws of reflection at a concave mirror, and yet the reflected beams do not stay parallel.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: True. Each ray follows the laws of reflection at the point where it strikes. But the surface of a concave mirror is curved, so the rays strike it at places where it faces different ways, and the reflected rays come closer together (converge) instead of staying parallel. Obeying the laws does not mean the beam stays parallel; that happens only with a plane mirror.
s: verdict: true
reason: each ray obeys the laws, but the curved surface sends the rays in directions that converge

questions.q: On a sunny day, Sneha's concave mirror made a sheet of paper smoke within a few minutes. On a cloudy day, with the same mirror held steady and the paper at the distance of the smallest spot, she got only a dim spot and no smoke even after ten minutes. Explain the difference in three steps.
questions.a: 1. The mirror behaves the same on both days: a concave mirror converges whatever light falls on it into a small spot. 2. On the cloudy day much less sunlight reaches the mirror, so much less light is collected and brought to the spot (which is why the spot is dim). 3. The heat at the spot comes from the light concentrated there; with so little light concentrated, not enough heat is produced to make the paper smoke.
s: the mirror still converges whatever light falls on it
less sunlight reaches it on a cloudy day, so less light is concentrated (dim spot)
the heat comes from the concentrated light, so too little heat to make the paper smoke

questions.q: A teacher in Indore runs the activity of burning paper with sunlight and a concave mirror. Which of these steps by a student breaks the safety rules?
questions.a: Checking how bright the spot is by looking into the mirror
o: Checking how bright the spot is by looking into the mirror
Doing the activity only while the teacher is present
Directing the bright spot only onto a single sheet of newspaper
Keeping the bright spot well away from everyone's face

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Because every ray obeys the laws of reflection, a concave mirror sends back a parallel beam of light as a parallel beam.
Reason (R): Each ray of light that strikes a spherical mirror follows the laws of reflection.
questions.a: A is false, but R is true
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false

questions.q:
Match each observation in Column I with the best explanation in Column II.
Column I
1. The paper smokes only where the bright spot falls
2. The bright spot keeps drifting over the paper and nothing smokes
3. Concentrated sunlight boils a liquid in a solar plant
4. A furnace with many mirrors melts steel
Column II
a. The steam produced can be used to generate electricity
b. Concentrated light produces enough heat at that point
c. Solar furnaces concentrate sunlight strongly enough to melt steel
d. The concentrated light does not stay on one point long enough

Three mirrors of the same size, P, Q and R, were each held facing the Sun under a teacher's supervision, and a sheet of paper was held in the reflected light for five minutes. The paper was moved to different distances for each mirror. Results (illustrative):
P: at one distance, a tiny dazzling spot formed; the paper smoked after about two minutes.
Q: a patch of light about the size of the mirror at every distance; the paper only felt slightly warm.
R: a dim patch that grew larger as the paper was moved away from the mirror; the paper did not warm noticeably.
(a) Identify mirror P, with the reason.
(b) Identify mirror Q, with the reason.
(c) Identify mirror R, with the reason.
(d) Explain why R's patch grew larger as the paper moved away.
(e) All three mirrors received the same sunlight. Use the results to explain what, besides collecting sunlight, is needed to make paper smoke.
questions.a: (a) P is a concave mirror: it brought the reflected sunlight together into a tiny spot at one distance, which only a converging mirror does. (b) Q is a plane mirror: the reflected beams stayed parallel, so the patch kept the size of the mirror at every distance. (c) R is a convex mirror: the reflected light spread out. (d) A convex mirror makes the reflected beams diverge, so the farther the paper, the more the beams have spread apart and the larger (and dimmer) the patch. (e) The sunlight must be concentrated into a small area. Q and R collected as much sunlight as P but did not bring it together, so no point received enough heat; only P's converged, concentrated light produced enough heat to make the paper smoke.
s: (a) P concave: light converged to a tiny spot
(b) Q plane: beams stay parallel, patch the size of the mirror
(c) R convex: light spread out
(d) diverging beams spread more with distance, so the patch grows
(e) the light must be concentrated in a small area, not just collected

questions.q: A solar furnace uses many mirrors to melt steel, yet sunlight reflected by a single plane mirror onto a steel bar hardly warms it. What best explains the difference?
questions.a: The furnace's mirrors concentrate sunlight into a small area, producing great heat there
o: The furnace's mirrors concentrate sunlight into a small area, producing great heat there
The furnace's mirrors keep the sunlight parallel so that all of it reaches the steel
The furnace's mirrors spread the sunlight evenly over the steel so it heats evenly
The furnace's mirrors produce extra heat of their own whenever sunlight falls on them

questions.q:
Consider these statements about mirrors and sunlight.
Statement 1: A convex mirror makes the reflected beams of a parallel beam come closer together.
Statement 2: Holding the bright spot from a concave mirror steady on paper for a few minutes can make the paper smoke, because concentrated light produces heat there.
Statement 3: A large plane mirror can burn paper just like a concave mirror, since it also reflects sunlight.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A student's notebook has only this observation: 'The reflected beams got closer and closer together and met near one small bright spot.' Work backwards: describe the set-up that most likely produced it (what kind of light fell on what kind of mirror), and predict one thing that would happen if the same set-up were used with sunlight and a sheet of paper held at the spot.
questions.a: Set-up: several parallel beams of light (for example from a torch and a comb with many openings) falling on a concave mirror, because only a concave mirror makes parallel reflected beams come closer together, converge; a plane mirror keeps them parallel and a convex mirror spreads them. With sunlight, the concave mirror would concentrate the light into a small bright spot on the paper; held steady for a few minutes (under supervision), this produces enough heat to make the paper smoke or catch fire.
s: parallel beams as the light falling on the mirror
a concave mirror, since only it converges parallel beams
prediction: sunlight concentrated to a bright spot that can make the paper smoke

questions.q:
(a) The chapter says solar concentrators use two kinds of devices to bring sunlight into a small area. Name them.
(b) A designer offers to build a cheap concentrator from convex mirrors. Using what a convex mirror does to a parallel beam, explain why it would fail.
questions.a: (a) Mirrors and lenses. (b) A convex mirror makes the reflected parallel beams spread apart (diverge), so the sunlight would be spread over a larger area instead of being concentrated into a small one; no hot spot would form.
s: (a) mirrors and lenses
(b) a convex mirror diverges the beams, spreading the light instead of concentrating it

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Thane used a torch and a comb with many openings uncovered to send several parallel beams of light onto three mirrors, one after another, and recorded what the reflected beams did on a sheet of paper close to each mirror.
Plane mirror: the reflected beams stayed parallel.
Concave mirror: the reflected beams spread apart.
Convex mirror: the reflected beams came closer together.
(a) Two entries in the record have been swapped. Identify them and correct them.
(b) Using the corrected record, predict what the group would see from the convex mirror on a second sheet placed much farther away than the first, and explain.
(c) Next day only the plane mirror and the convex mirror are available, and the group wants to make paper smoke in sunlight. Decide whether either mirror can do it, and suggest what the group could usefully show with them instead.
questions.a: (a) The concave and convex entries are swapped: a concave mirror makes the reflected beams come closer together (converge), and a convex mirror makes them spread apart (diverge). (b) The beams would be even farther apart, because diverging beams keep spreading as they travel away from the mirror. (c) Neither can: a plane mirror keeps the reflected beams parallel and a convex mirror spreads them, so neither concentrates sunlight into a small spot, and only concentrated light produces enough heat to make paper smoke. They could instead show the contrast between the two mirrors (parallel beams staying parallel versus spreading out), or wait for a concave mirror or a convex lens.
s: (a) concave and convex entries swapped: concave converges, convex diverges
(b) farther apart still, since diverging beams keep spreading
(c) neither concentrates light, so neither can make paper smoke; show parallel versus diverging instead

questions.q: A square concave mirror, 30 cm by 30 cm, collects sunlight and concentrates it into a square spot 3 cm by 3 cm on a sheet of paper. About how many times as much sunlight falls on each square centimetre of the spot as on a square centimetre of paper in ordinary sunlight?
questions.a: 100 times
o: 100 times
10 times
900 times
30 times

questions.q:
In the parallel-beam activity, the beams falling on each mirror must be parallel to begin with.
(a) What does a plane mirror do to such beams, and why does that make it a useful comparison?
(b) Using (a), explain why the activity would prove nothing about a convex mirror if the beams were already spreading out before they reached it.
questions.a: (a) A plane mirror reflects parallel beams as parallel beams, so it shows what happens when the mirror itself adds no converging or spreading. (b) A convex mirror is shown to diverge light by turning parallel beams into spreading ones. If the beams were spreading before reaching it, spreading after reflection could simply be the spreading they already had, so it would not show what the mirror did.
s: (a) a plane mirror keeps parallel beams parallel, showing a mirror that adds no change
(b) beams already spreading would hide whether the convex mirror caused the spreading

questions.q:
Two square concave mirrors, one 10 cm by 10 cm and one 40 cm by 40 cm, each bring sunlight to a bright spot of the same size on paper.
(a) How many times as much sunlight does the larger mirror collect?
(b) Using (a), predict which sheet of paper will start to smoke first, and explain.
questions.a: (a) The areas are 40 x 40 = 1600 square cm and 10 x 10 = 100 square cm, so the larger mirror collects 1600 / 100 = 16 times as much sunlight. (b) The paper at the larger mirror's spot: both spots are the same size, but 16 times as much light is concentrated into it, so more heat is produced there and the paper smokes sooner.
s: (b) larger mirror's paper, since more light is concentrated into the same-sized spot, giving more heat

questions.q:
A farmers' co-operative in Barmer, Rajasthan, wants to use sunlight for large-scale cooking in its community kitchen.
(a) Which kind of spherical mirror should its solar concentrator use? Give the reason.
(b) One member suggests laying many plane mirrors flat on the ground, side by side, all facing straight up at the Sun. Explain why this arrangement will not concentrate the sunlight.
(c) In a trial with one concave mirror (illustrative): a pot of water placed at the small, sharp spot boiled in 25 minutes; the same pot placed 40 cm nearer the mirror, where the light formed a wide patch, only became warm in the same time. Explain the difference.
(d) The concentrator can be set up at one of two sites, and its stand cannot be made any firmer.
Site A: sunny for about 9 hours a day, but strong gusts often make the stand sway.
Site B: sunny for about 7 hours a day, sheltered and calm.
Decide which site to choose, using what the trial and the sunlight activity show.
questions.a: (a) Concave mirrors, because a concave mirror converges parallel beams of light such as sunlight, concentrating the light into a small area where it produces heat. (b) Each plane mirror reflects the parallel sunlight as parallel beams, and flat mirrors all facing the same way send the light back in the same direction, still parallel; it is never brought together into a small area. (c) At the sharp spot the light is concentrated into a small area, so a lot of heat is produced on the pot; at the wide patch the same light is spread over a larger area, so much less heat reaches each part of the pot. (d) Site B. The trial shows that the pot heats well only while it stays at the concentrated spot, and the sunlight activity needs the mirror and paper held steady. At Site A the swaying stand keeps moving the spot off the pot, so the extra two hours of sunshine are of little use; at Site B the spot stays on the pot for all 7 hours.
s: (a) concave, because it converges sunlight into a small area
(b) flat plane mirrors keep the reflected beams parallel, so the light is never concentrated
(c) at the sharp spot light is concentrated (more heat); in the wide patch it is spread out
(d) Site B, because the spot must stay steady on the pot; swaying at A wastes its extra sunshine

questions.q: Priya says, 'If I use a plane mirror that is as big as the concave mirror, it will collect just as much sunlight, so it will burn the paper just as well.' Is Priya right? Give your verdict and explain using what each mirror does to a parallel beam.
questions.a: No. Sunlight reaching the mirror is a parallel beam. A plane mirror reflects parallel beams as parallel beams, so the reflected light lands on the paper spread over a patch about the size of the mirror and is not concentrated. A concave mirror makes the reflected beams converge, so the same light is concentrated into a small bright spot, and it is this concentration that produces enough heat to ignite paper. Collecting the same light is not enough; it has to be brought together.
s: verdict: no
plane mirror keeps the reflected beams parallel, so light is not concentrated
concave mirror converges light into a small spot; concentration produces the heat

questions.q: Rahul repeats the sunlight activity with a convex mirror instead of a concave one, under his teacher's supervision. What will he find?
questions.a: The reflected light spreads out, so no bright spot forms and the paper does not burn
o: The reflected light spreads out, so no bright spot forms and the paper does not burn
The paper burns faster, because the bulging surface faces the Sun more fully
A bright spot forms, but only when the paper is held very much farther from the mirror
A bright spot forms, but it is cooler because a convex mirror reflects less

questions.q:
In the parallel-beam activity, most openings of the comb are left uncovered instead of just one.
(a) What do the many openings give that a single slit does not?
(b) Using (a), explain why a single slit could never show that a concave mirror converges light.
questions.a: (a) Many openings give several parallel beams side by side at the same time. (b) Converging means the reflected beams come closer to one another; with a single beam there is nothing for it to come closer to, so you can only see one beam obeying the laws of reflection, not the beams getting closer together.
s: (a) several parallel beams at once
(b) converging is about beams getting closer to each other, which one beam cannot show

questions.q:
Four groups in a school in Vadodara did the sunlight activity at the same time with identical concave mirrors and thin paper. Their notes:
Group 1: spot about 4 mm wide; held mirror and paper steady; paper smoked after 2 minutes.
Group 2: patch about 20 mm wide; held steady; no smoke after 5 minutes.
Group 3: spot about 4 mm wide; the paper kept shaking in the wind; no smoke after 5 minutes.
Group 4: spot about 4 mm wide; held steady; paper smoked after 2 minutes; members took turns looking into the mirror to aim the spot.
(a) Explain Group 2's result and what they should have done.
(b) Explain Group 3's result.
(c) Group 4 got the same result as Group 1. Explain why their method still cannot be accepted.
(d) The teacher will display one group's method as the model. Decide which group, and justify by ranking the other three by what went wrong.
questions.a: (a) A 20 mm patch means the paper was not at the distance that gives a small, sharp spot, so the light was not concentrated enough; they should have adjusted the distance of the paper until the spot was small and sharp. (b) The spot kept moving over the paper, so the concentrated light did not stay on one point long enough to produce the heat needed; the activity requires the mirror and paper to be held steady for a few minutes. (c) Looking into the mirror that is reflecting the Sun breaks the safety rule; a method that risks the eyes cannot be the model, whatever the result. (d) Group 1, which used the right distance, held steady and followed the safety rules. Group 4 is the most serious problem because it broke a safety rule; Groups 2 and 3 made method slips (wrong paper distance, not held steady) that only spoiled the result.
s: (a) paper not at the sharp-spot distance; adjust until the spot is small and sharp
(b) spot moved, so heat did not build at one point; must be held steady
(c) looking into the mirror reflecting the Sun breaks the safety rule
(d) Group 1 as the model, with Group 4's safety breach ranked worse than the method slips of Groups 2 and 3

questions.q: Doing the sunlight activity with a concave mirror under her teacher's supervision, Tanvi sees only a large, blurry patch of light on her paper. What should she do next?
questions.a: Move the paper nearer to or farther from the mirror until the spot is small and sharp
o: Move the paper nearer to or farther from the mirror until the spot is small and sharp
Turn the mirror's reflecting surface away from the Sun and try again
Swap the concave mirror for a convex mirror, since its bulging face gathers more sunlight
Look into the mirror to see exactly where the reflected light is going

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Bhubaneswar made three water drops on a clear plastic strip placed over the same line of small print.
Drop 1: placed on a spot rubbed with a thin coat of oil; it formed a round drop curving outward; the letters under it looked larger than the letters nearby.
Drop 2: placed on a clean, unoiled spot; it spread out into a thin flat film; the letters under it looked the same as the letters nearby.
Drop 3: placed on a spot rubbed with wax, but far too much water was poured on, and it spread into a flat puddle; the letters under it looked the same as the letters nearby.
(a) Explain why Drop 2 did not change the size of the letters.
(b) Drop 3 sat on wax, yet it behaved like Drop 2. What does this show about what really makes a drop act as a lens?
(c) The group wants one drop as a tiny magnifier for reading a seed packet, without remaking any drop. Decide which drop to use, and explain what the oil or wax is for.
questions.a: (a) Drop 2 spread into a flat film, so its surface was not curved; a flat transparent layer behaves like a window pane and does not change the size of things seen through it. (b) The coating alone is not enough: what makes a drop act as a lens is a curved (outward-curving) surface. Drop 3 ended up flat, so, like Drop 2, it could not enlarge the letters. (c) Drop 1, the only drop that is round and curved outward, so it acts like a simple lens and makes print appear larger, as a magnifying glass does. The oil or wax helps a small drop of water form a nice round drop instead of spreading flat.
s: (a) a flat film has no curved surface, so it acts like a window pane: no size change
(b) the curved surface, not the coating, makes a drop a lens; Drop 3 was flat
(c) Drop 1, the only curved drop; oil or wax helps a small drop stay round

questions.q: Mohan says, 'A convex lens always makes things look bigger, so a magnifying glass will enlarge anything, at any distance.' Is the word 'always' in his claim correct? Give your verdict and explain how the view through a convex lens changes with the distance of the object.
questions.a: No. Close behind a convex lens (such as a magnifying glass), an object appears erect and enlarged. But as the distance between the object and the lens increases, the object appears inverted; it is enlarged at first and then diminishes. So far enough away the object looks inverted and smaller, and a convex lens does not always make things look bigger.
s: verdict: no, 'always' is wrong
close behind a convex lens the object looks erect and enlarged
farther away it turns inverted and then diminishes, so it is not always bigger

questions.q: Bina places a small drop of water on an oiled plastic scale over a printed page. The drop's surface curves outward, so it is thicker in the middle than at its edges. How will the letters under the drop look, and why?
questions.a: Larger, because the drop acts like a convex lens
o: Larger, because the drop acts like a convex lens
Smaller, because the drop acts like a convex mirror
Unchanged, because water is clear like a window pane
Larger, because the drop reflects them like a concave mirror

questions.q: Leela tests four things over a line of small print: a flat glass window pane, a magnifying glass, a lens thicker at its edges than at its middle, and a water drop curved outward on an oiled strip. The number of these four that can make the letters look larger is ___. (Write a number.)
Looking through a lens, Kunal sees a toy kept 5 cm behind it erect and smaller, and again erect and a little different in size when the toy is 50 cm behind it. Which lens is he using?
questions.a: A concave lens
o: A concave lens
A convex lens, as the size changes with distance
A flat glass plate, as the toy stays erect
A convex lens with the toy kept far away

questions.q:
Five transparent or shiny objects are placed, one at a time, on or just above a line of small print.
(a) A clear glass marble
(b) A spectacle lens that is thicker at its edges than at its middle
(c) A polished steel katori, turned upside down
(d) A flat piece of window glass
(e) A round drop of water, curving outward, on an oiled plastic sheet
For each one, say whether it acts as a lens, name the type where it is one, and say what the print looks like through it (or why the print cannot be seen through it).
questions.a: (a) A lens: transparent with curved surfaces and thicker at the middle, so it acts as a convex lens; print close beneath it looks erect and larger. (b) A lens: transparent, curved and thicker at the edges, so a concave lens; the print looks erect and smaller. (c) Not a lens: steel is not transparent, so the print cannot be seen through it; its shiny curved surface acts as a mirror instead. (d) Not a lens: its surfaces are flat, so the print looks the same size and shape, as through a window pane. (e) Acts as a simple lens: its surface curves outward (thicker in the middle), so the letters under it look larger, as with a magnifying glass.
s: (a) convex lens: print erect and larger
(b) concave lens: print erect and smaller
(c) not a lens: not transparent; it reflects like a mirror
(d) not a lens: flat surfaces, print unchanged
(e) acts as a simple lens curving outward: letters larger

questions.q: Through an unknown lens, Riya sees a tree far away upside down. Show that this lens cannot be thicker at its edges than at its middle.
questions.a: A lens thicker at the edges than at the middle is a concave lens. An object seen through a concave lens always appears erect (and diminished), at every distance, so a concave lens can never show the tree upside down. Since Riya sees an inverted tree, the lens must be a convex lens (an object farther from a convex lens appears inverted), and a convex lens is thicker at the middle than at its edges. So the lens cannot be thicker at its edges.
s: thicker at the edges means a concave lens
a concave lens always gives an erect view, so it cannot show the tree inverted
so the lens is convex, which is thicker at the middle, not the edges

questions.q:
In a lens activity, a small toy is placed upright and a lens is fixed in a holder.
(a) Where must the toy and Sunil's eye be, relative to the lens, for him to see the toy through it?
(b) Using (a), explain how this is different from looking at the same toy in a mirror.
questions.a: (a) On opposite sides: the toy behind the lens and his eye on the other side, looking through the lens. (b) A lens lets light from the toy pass through it to his eye on the other side, but a mirror reflects light back, so with a mirror the toy and his eye are on the same side and he sees the image in the mirror.
s: (a) toy and eye on opposite sides of the lens
(b) the lens passes light through, while a mirror reflects it back so object and eye are on the same side

questions.q:
(a) From this list, pick out every item that is a lens: a flat clear plastic ruler; a clear glass bead that is thicker at the middle than at its edges; a piece of curved, polished steel; a clear plastic disc that is thicker at its edges than at its middle.
(b) Name each lens you picked as convex or concave.
questions.a: (a) The glass bead and the plastic disc: each is a transparent material with curved surfaces. The flat ruler has no curved surfaces, and the curved steel is not transparent (it is a curved mirror, which reflects light). (b) The glass bead is a convex lens (thicker at the middle); the plastic disc is a concave lens (thicker at the edges).
s: (a) the bead and the disc, because they are transparent with curved surfaces (ruler flat, steel not transparent)
(b) bead convex, disc concave

questions.q:
Consider these statements about lenses.
Statement 1: A lens can be made of plastic as well as of glass.
Statement 2: Like mirrors, lenses can be either convex or concave.
Statement 3: A clear plastic disc that is thicker at its middle than at its edges is a convex lens.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only
2 only

questions.q: A glass workshop has a flat piece of window glass. Which change would turn it into a lens?
questions.a: Grinding it so that its surfaces become curved
o: Grinding it so that its surfaces become curved
Making it thicker while keeping both faces flat
Coating one face of it with a thin aluminium layer
Cutting it into a neat circle with smooth edges

questions.q:
A stamp club in Pune tests four transparent pieces, W, X, Y and Z, by viewing the same small stamp kept 3 cm behind each piece. They record how large the stamp looks compared with its real size (illustrative values); in every case the stamp looks erect.
W: 1.0 times (same size)
X: 2.5 times
Y: 1.5 times
Z: 0.6 times
(a) Which piece is a concave lens, and which is most likely a flat glass plate? Give reasons.
(b) Which pieces would show the stamp inverted if it were moved far away from them? Explain.
(c) A member says W must be a weak lens. Use what the chapter says about a flat window pane to judge this.
(d) The club wants the biggest erect view of a stamp held close. Decide which piece to use and give one instruction the user must follow to keep the view erect.
questions.a: (a) Z is the concave lens: it is the only one that makes the close stamp look smaller (erect and diminished), as a concave lens always does. W is most likely the flat glass plate, because it leaves the size unchanged. (b) X and Y: they make the close stamp look erect and enlarged, so they are convex lenses, and as the distance from a convex lens increases the object appears inverted. Z (concave) and W (flat) keep the stamp erect. (c) Not justified: a flat transparent glass such as a window pane makes objects look the same size and shape, which is exactly what W shows; there is no evidence of a curved surface. (d) X, which gives the largest erect view (2.5 times); the user must keep the stamp close behind it, because if the stamp is moved far away the view becomes inverted.
s: (a) Z concave (only one diminishing); W flat glass (no change)
(b) X and Y, as they are convex, and convex lenses invert far objects
(c) W behaves like a flat window pane, so 'weak lens' is not supported
(d) choose X and keep the stamp close, since far away the view turns inverted

questions.q: On a newspaper, Imran places a glass paperweight with a flat base and a dome-shaped top (thicker in the middle than at its rim), next to a flat glass coaster of the same thickness as the paperweight's rim. How do the letters look under each?
questions.a: Larger under the paperweight, unchanged under the coaster
o: Larger under the paperweight, unchanged under the coaster
Unchanged under both, since both are clear glass
Larger under both, since both are made of thick glass
Smaller under the domed paperweight, larger under the flat coaster

questions.q:
Varun says, 'A lens is just a curved mirror that you can see through.'
(a) Give one way in which lenses and curved mirrors really are alike.
(b) Give the most important way in which his description is wrong, and what it changes about where you must look from.
questions.a: (a) Like mirrors, lenses can be convex or concave, and both have curved surfaces that change the size and orientation of what you see. (b) A mirror reflects light, but a lens lets light pass through it; so we look at the object through a lens, from the other side of it, instead of seeing its image in the lens on the same side as the object.
s: (a) both are curved and come in convex and concave forms
(b) a lens lets light pass through rather than reflecting it, so we see through it from the far side

questions.q:
A watch repairer in Rajkot looks at a tiny gear through a magnifying glass held at different heights above it (illustrative values; 'times' compares the size seen with the real size).
2 cm: erect, about 1.7 times
4 cm: erect, 5 times
8 cm: inverted, about 1.7 times
15 cm: inverted, 0.5 times
(a) Which readings show that the magnifying glass is a convex lens? Explain.
(b) At which recorded height should she work, and why?
(c) Her apprentice holds the glass at 8 cm and says the gear is now 'upside down but still magnified, so it is fine'. Explain what has happened and why she would still not work at that height.
(d) Predict what she would see with the glass 25 cm above the gear, and justify.
(e) The apprentice offers a lens that is thicker at its edges, saying, 'I will just find the right height for it.' Judge his idea.
questions.a: (a) Close up (2 cm, 4 cm) the gear looks erect and enlarged, and farther away (8 cm, 15 cm) it looks inverted, first enlarged and then diminished. That is how an object looks through a convex lens. (b) 4 cm, which gives the largest erect view (5 times). (c) The glass is now far enough from the gear for the view through a convex lens to turn inverted; it is still enlarged at this height but will diminish if raised further, and an upside-down view makes left and right, up and down confusing to work with, so 4 cm is better. (d) Inverted and smaller than at 15 cm (less than 0.5 times), because once the view is inverted it keeps diminishing as the distance increases. (e) His idea fails: a lens thicker at the edges is a concave lens, and an object seen through a concave lens always appears erect and diminished, at every distance, so no height will magnify the gear.
s: (a) erect and enlarged close up, inverted farther away: convex lens
(b) 4 cm, the largest erect view
(c) the view has turned inverted at this distance (still enlarged, will diminish); an inverted view is awkward to work with
(d) inverted and smaller than 0.5 times
(e) wrong: a concave lens always gives an erect, diminished view

questions.q: True or false? 'A magnifying glass makes print look bigger simply because its glass is thick, so a thick flat slab of glass would work just as well.' Give your verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. What matters is the shape: a magnifying glass is a convex lens, with curved surfaces and thicker at the middle than at the edges. A flat piece of glass, however thick, has no curved surfaces, so, like a window pane, it leaves things looking the same size and shape.
s: verdict: false
reason: curved surfaces (thicker in the middle) make it magnify; flat glass of any thickness leaves the size unchanged

questions.q:
(a) Looking through a flat glass window pane, Zoya sees the trees outside at their usual size and shape. What about the glass explains this?
(b) Using (a), state what would have to be different about the glass for the trees to look larger or smaller, and what the glass would then be called.
questions.a: (a) The glass is transparent and its surfaces are flat, not curved, so objects seen through it look the same size and shape. (b) Its surfaces would have to be curved; a piece of transparent material with curved surfaces is a lens.
s: (a) transparent with flat surfaces, so no change in size or shape
(b) curved surfaces are needed; the glass would then be a lens

questions.q:
A lab assistant measures the thickness of four clear glass pieces at the middle, halfway out and at the edge (in mm).
P: 5, 4, 2
Q: 2, 3, 5
R: 3, 3, 3
S: 4, 3.5, 1
(a) Classify each piece.
(b) Which pieces could be used as a magnifying glass?
(c) Which pieces can never make print look bigger, and why?
questions.a: (a) P and S are convex lenses (thicker at the middle than at the edges); Q is a concave lens (thicker at the edges); R is a flat glass plate, not a lens (the same thickness throughout, no curved surfaces). (b) P and S: a convex lens held close to print shows it erect and enlarged. (c) Q and R: through a concave lens objects always appear erect and diminished, and a flat plate, like a window pane, leaves the size unchanged.
s: (a) P and S convex, Q concave, R flat plate (not a lens)
(b) P and S, as convex lenses enlarge print held close
(c) Q (always diminished) and R (no change)

questions.q: Dadi uses a magnifying glass to read the small print on a medicine strip. Which statement about what is happening is NOT correct?
questions.a: She sees the letters in the glass, as an image formed by reflection
o: She sees the letters in the glass, as an image formed by reflection
The glass is a lens that is thicker at the middle than at the edges
Light from the strip passes through the glass to reach her eyes
Held close to the strip, it shows the letters erect and enlarged

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Held close to a line of print, a magnifying glass makes the letters look bigger.
Reason (R): A magnifying glass is a convex lens, and an object close behind a convex lens appears erect and enlarged.
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true

questions.q:
A Class 8 group in Kolkata made a poster titled 'Lenses around us'. It has five claims.
Claim 1: Eyeglasses are curved mirrors that help people see clearly.
Claim 2: A smartphone camera can work without any lens.
Claim 3: Telescopes can use lenses, but most modern telescopes use a large concave mirror as their main mirror.
Claim 4: A microscope uses lenses to work.
Claim 5: Because a convex lens converges sunlight, nobody should ever look at the Sun through one.
Judge each claim as correct or wrong, giving the reason from the chapter, and correct every wrong claim.
questions.a: Claim 1 wrong: eyeglasses are lenses, through which light passes, not mirrors. Claim 2 wrong: cameras, including smartphone cameras, use lenses to work. Claim 3 correct: the chapter says telescopes use lenses, and also that most modern telescopes are reflecting telescopes whose main mirror is a large concave mirror. Claim 4 correct: microscopes use lenses to work. Claim 5 correct: a convex lens concentrates sunlight into a small area, and looking at the Sun directly or through the lens may damage the eyes.
s: Claim 1 wrong: eyeglasses are lenses
Claim 2 wrong: cameras use lenses
Claim 3 correct: lenses, or a large concave main mirror in most modern telescopes
Claim 4 correct: microscopes use lenses
Claim 5 correct: converged sunlight can damage the eyes

questions.q: For the lens activity, a lens is fixed upright between two books, and white sheets are spread over both books, so there is paper on both sides of the lens. Why is paper needed on both sides?
questions.a: To see the paths of the beams both before and after the lens
o: To see the paths of the beams both before and after the lens
To reflect the beams back through the lens for a second time
To stop the two books from scattering the parallel beams
To make the beams brighter so that the lens can bend them

questions.q:
In the lens activity, the parallel beams are passed through a thin glass plate first, before the convex and concave lenses.
(a) What does the glass plate show?
(b) Using (a), explain what the lens results can then be put down to.
questions.a: (a) That the beams pass through a flat piece of transparent glass as they are, without coming together or spreading out. (b) Since flat glass changes nothing, the converging (convex lens) and diverging (concave lens) must be caused by the curved surfaces of the lenses, not simply by light passing through glass.
s: (a) flat glass lets the beams pass unchanged
(b) so converging or diverging is due to the lens's curved surfaces

questions.q: Kiran says, 'A convex lens and a concave mirror both bring parallel light together, so either one could be used in a device that concentrates sunlight.' Is Kiran right? Give your verdict with the evidence from the chapter.
questions.a: Yes. A concave mirror converges parallel beams on reflection, and a convex lens converges parallel beams passing through it; each can concentrate sunlight into a small area and make paper burn. The chapter says solar concentrators concentrate sunlight into a small area using mirrors and lenses, so either kind of converging device can be used.
s: verdict: yes
both converge light: the concave mirror by reflection, the convex lens as light passes through
solar concentrators use mirrors and lenses

questions.q:
Match each item in Column I with the description in Column II that fits it.
Column I
1. Thin transparent glass plate
2. Convex lens
3. Concave lens
4. A smartphone camera
Column II
a. A device the chapter says needs lenses to work
b. Lets parallel beams pass through as they are
c. Is called a diverging lens
d. Is called a converging lens

Parallel beams of light are sent, one at a time, onto five things: a thin glass plate, a convex lens, a concave lens, a concave mirror and a plane mirror. The number of these that make the beams either come together or spread apart is ___. (Write a number.)

Consider these statements about lenses and parallel beams of light.
Statement 1: A concave lens is also called a diverging lens.
Statement 2: Parallel beams passing through a thin glass plate come out as they went in.
Statement 3: Parallel beams passing through a convex lens spread farther apart.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
2 only
2 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
(a) In the sunlight activity with a concave mirror, and in the repeat with a convex lens, on which side of the mirror and of the lens must the paper be held?
(b) Using (a), explain the difference in terms of what each does to light.
questions.a: (a) With the concave mirror, the paper is held on the same side as the Sun (in front of the reflecting surface); with the convex lens, it is held on the far side of the lens, away from the Sun. (b) A mirror reflects the light back, so it converges on the side the light came from; a lens lets light pass through it, so it converges on the other side.

questions.q:
A government school in Puri can buy only one demonstration kit this year for its Class 8 light lessons: Kit A has a large convex lens; Kit B has a large concave mirror of the same size. The school already owns a magnifying glass (a convex lens) and a plane mirror. The teacher wants the new kit to (i) show sunlight being concentrated to make paper smoke, and (ii) add something the school cannot already show.
(a) Show that both kits can do job (i).
(b) Name one chapter idea that Kit A would add which the school cannot already show with what it owns.
(c) Name one chapter idea that Kit B would add which the school cannot already show.
(d) Decide which kit the school should buy, and justify using (b) and (c).
questions.a: (a) Both converge parallel sunlight into a small, bright spot: the concave mirror by reflection, the convex lens as the light passes through, so both can make paper smoke (under supervision). (b) None: the magnifying glass the school owns is already a convex lens, so it can already show magnifying, seeing through a lens, inverted views of far objects, converging a beam and even burning paper; Kit A adds nothing new apart from its size. (c) Any concave-mirror idea, for example: a parallel beam converging on reflection; an image seen in the mirror that is erect and enlarged close up and inverted farther away (as with a dental mirror); the reflector of a torch or headlight. The plane mirror the school owns cannot show any of these. (d) Kit B: it does job (i) as well as Kit A, and unlike Kit A it adds concave-mirror ideas the school has no other way to show.
s: (a) both converge sunlight to a small spot (mirror by reflection, lens by passing light through)
(b) Kit A adds nothing new, because the owned magnifying glass is already a convex lens
(c) a valid concave-mirror idea the plane mirror cannot show
(d) Kit B, because it does (i) and adds what the school lacks

questions.a: True. A concave lens is a diverging lens: parallel beams passing through it spread apart. A convex mirror also makes parallel beams diverge, but on reflection. The way they handle light differs (passing through versus reflecting back), but both spread the beam out.

reason: a concave lens diverges light passing through; a convex mirror diverges it on reflection

questions.q:
A bundle of parallel beams 6 cm wide is sent at six devices, one at a time. The table gives where the light goes and the width of the bundle 20 cm from the device (illustrative values).
Thin glass plate: goes on to the far side; 6 cm
Plane mirror: comes back to the side it came from; 6 cm
Convex lens: goes on to the far side; 1 cm
Concave mirror: comes back; 1.5 cm
Concave lens: goes on to the far side; 10 cm
Convex mirror: comes back; 9 cm
(a) Which devices converge the beams? Use the widths.
(b) Which devices diverge the beams?
(c) Which two leave the beams as they were, and how do you know?
(d) Using the 'where the light goes' column, explain which devices are lenses or plates and which are mirrors.
(e) Ali concludes, 'So the word concave always means converging.' Use the table to judge him.
questions.a: (a) The convex lens and the concave mirror: the bundle narrows from 6 cm to 1 cm and 1.5 cm. (b) The concave lens and the convex mirror: the bundle widens to 10 cm and 9 cm. (c) The thin glass plate and the plane mirror: the bundle stays 6 cm wide, so the beams stay parallel. (d) The plate and the two lenses let the light pass on to the far side, because light passes through them; the three mirrors send the light back to the side it came from, because a mirror reflects light. (e) Ali is wrong: the concave mirror converges (6 cm to 1.5 cm), but the concave lens diverges (6 cm to 10 cm); for lenses it is the convex one that converges.
s: (a) convex lens and concave mirror (bundle narrows)
(b) concave lens and convex mirror (bundle widens)
(c) plate and plane mirror: width unchanged, beams stay parallel
(d) far side means light passed through (plate, lenses); coming back means reflection (mirrors)
(e) wrong: the concave lens widens the bundle; only the concave mirror converges

questions.q:
Sort these six things into three groups: (i) works using lenses, (ii) works using curved mirrors, (iii) the chapter says it can use either. Give a reason for each group.
Eyeglasses; a smartphone camera; a microscope; a torch reflector; a vehicle's side-view mirror; a telescope.
questions.a: (i) Lenses: eyeglasses, the smartphone camera and the microscope; the chapter says eyeglasses are lenses and that cameras and microscopes use lenses to work. (ii) Curved mirrors: the torch reflector (concave) and the side-view mirror (convex); both reflect light. (iii) Either: the telescope; the chapter says telescopes use lenses, and also that most modern telescopes are reflecting telescopes whose main mirror is a large concave mirror.
s: lenses: eyeglasses, smartphone camera, microscope
curved mirrors: torch reflector (concave) and side-view mirror (convex)
either: telescope, which can use lenses or a large concave main mirror

questions.q:
(a) To see a near book and then a far hill clearly, what does the lens in our eye do?
(b) Using (a), explain how this differs from what a person must do with a magnifying glass to keep small print looking erect and enlarged.
questions.a: (a) The eye's convex lens changes its own shape, which allows us to read a book or see something far away. (b) A magnifying glass cannot change its shape; to keep the print erect and enlarged the person must move the glass, keeping the print close behind it, because if the distance becomes larger the print appears inverted.
s: (a) the eye's convex lens changes its shape for near and far
(b) a magnifying glass has a fixed shape, so it must be moved to keep the print close

questions.q:
A science club in Coimbatore holds four transparent pieces, each 5 cm wide, in sunlight, one at a time, under their teacher's supervision. They measure the width of the patch of light on a sheet of paper held first 10 cm and then 20 cm below each piece (illustrative values). Over this range, light passing through a converging piece is still coming together.
Piece K: 5 cm at 10 cm; 5 cm at 20 cm
Piece L: 2.8 cm at 10 cm; 0.6 cm at 20 cm
Piece M: 7 cm at 10 cm; 9 cm at 20 cm
Piece N: 3.2 cm at 10 cm; 1.4 cm at 20 cm
(a) Which piece is the thin glass plate? Use both readings.
(b) Which piece is the concave lens? Use both readings.
(c) Rank L and N by how strongly the light is concentrated on the paper at 20 cm, and explain what this means for heating.
(d) The paper must stay 20 cm below the piece, and they want it to start smoking as soon as possible. Decide which piece to use, and state the safety rule that applies.
questions.a: (a) K: the patch is the same width as the piece (5 cm) at both distances, so the beams passed through as they were and stayed parallel, which is what a thin glass plate does. (b) M: the patch is wider than the piece and grows from 7 cm to 9 cm as the paper moves away, so the light is spreading out (diverging), which is what a concave lens does. L and N shrink with distance, so they converge: both are convex lenses. (c) L concentrates more than N: at 20 cm the same width of sunlight is squeezed into a 0.6 cm patch against 1.4 cm, so more light falls on each part of it and more heat is produced there. (d) Piece L, because at 20 cm it gives the smallest, most concentrated spot. Safety: never look at the Sun directly or through the lens, as it may damage the eyes (and keep the spot away from everyone).
s: (a) K: patch equals the piece's width at both distances, so beams pass unchanged
(b) M: patch wider than the piece and growing with distance, so light diverges
(c) L more concentrated than N at 20 cm (0.6 cm against 1.4 cm), so more heat
(d) choose L, with the rule: never look at the Sun directly or through the lens

questions.q: Show that a lens which makes a parallel beam of light spread apart cannot be the lens in a magnifying glass.
questions.a: A lens that makes a parallel beam spread apart is a diverging lens, that is, a concave lens. An object seen through a concave lens always appears erect and diminished, whatever its distance. A magnifying glass must make small print appear bigger, which needs a convex lens held close to the print (erect and enlarged). So a diverging lens can never act as a magnifying glass.
s: a beam-spreading lens is a diverging, concave lens
a concave lens always makes things look erect and diminished
a magnifying glass must enlarge, which needs a convex lens, so it cannot be this lens
